VBO:0000661.summary: The Broholmer is a large Danish mastiff with an old-estate silhouette: broad, substantial, and more quietly imposing than flashy. The modern breed was rebuilt from a very small population in the 1970s, so its story is as much about careful revival as it is about the manor houses and guarding work behind the name.
VBO:0000661.interestingFact: The breed takes its name from Broholm, the Danish estate associated with Count Niels Frederik Sehested and the nineteenth-century effort to establish the type.
VBO:0000661.historicalRoots: Danish estate and guard dog; modern revival began in the 1970s.

VBO:0200088.summary: The Australian Cattle Dog is a compact, weather-ready drover built for moving cattle across enormous distances. Its alert expression, strong outline, and blue- or red-speckled coat make it instantly recognizable. Breed standards often describe a watchful, energetic worker—but every individual dog still brings its own temperament to the job.
VBO:0200088.interestingFact: The nickname “heeler” comes from the breed’s traditional habit of controlling cattle by working low around their heels.
VBO:0200088.historicalRoots: Developed in Australia for long-distance cattle work.

VBO:0200108.summary: The Azawakh is a tall, exquisitely lean sighthound from the Sahel, with long legs, a tucked waist, and a silhouette that looks drawn in a single elegant line. It developed alongside pastoral communities including the Tuareg, and its history joins swift pursuit with life as a close camp companion.
VBO:0200108.interestingFact: An Azawakh’s spare build is not an unfinished look—it is a defining feature of a desert-adapted sighthound whose muscles and bone structure remain clearly visible.
VBO:0200108.historicalRoots: Sahelian sighthound associated with pastoral communities of Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso.

VBO:0200120.summary: The Basenji is a small, fine-boned hunting dog from Central Africa, famous for its curled tail, wrinkled brow, and unusually economical movement. It is often called “barkless,” though silence is not really the point: Basenjis have a distinctive voice all their own, along with a very ancient hunting-dog history.
VBO:0200120.interestingFact: Instead of a conventional bark, many Basenjis make a rising, yodel-like sound often called a baroo, shaped in part by the breed’s larynx.
VBO:0200120.historicalRoots: Central African hunting dog with long-established regional roots.

VBO:0200185.summary: The Boerboel is a powerful South African farm mastiff, squarely built and unmistakably substantial. Its history is tied to homesteads where a versatile large dog was expected to watch, accompany, and work around the property. That working background explains the serious outline better than any one-size-fits-all personality label could.
VBO:0200185.interestingFact: Its Afrikaans name combines “boer,” meaning farmer, with a word for a large dog—an unusually direct description of the breed’s original setting.
VBO:0200185.historicalRoots: South African farm and homestead dog developed from large guardian types.

VBO:0200231.summary: The Brazilian Terrier is a brisk, fine-boned little terrier with a mostly white coat, crisp tricolor markings, and a ready-for-anything outline. Developed in Brazil, it became a practical farm and household dog whose small size belied its usefulness around vermin. It is lively in appearance without needing cartoonish copy to sell the point.
VBO:0200231.interestingFact: The breed is one of Brazil’s internationally recognized native breeds, and its color pattern gives nearly every face a slightly different graphic mask.
VBO:0200231.historicalRoots: Brazilian farm terrier shaped by imported terriers and local selection.

VBO:0200338.summary: The Chihuahua packs an enormous visual identity into the smallest recognized dog-breed frame: round or deer-like head shapes, luminous eyes, and either a smooth or long coat. Its modern name comes from the Mexican state of Chihuahua, while its deeper ancestry is often connected—carefully, not conclusively—to earlier companion dogs of Mexico.
VBO:0200338.interestingFact: Smooth- and long-coated Chihuahuas belong to the same breed, so coat length can change the entire first impression without changing the essential tiny silhouette.
VBO:0200338.historicalRoots: Mexican companion breed with debated links to pre-Columbian small dogs.

VBO:0200345.summary: The Chinese Crested turns contrast into a whole breed: the hairless variety carries silky furnishings on the head, feet, and tail, while the Powderpuff wears a complete soft coat. Both can appear in the same litter. The result is less “two different dogs” than two dramatic expressions of one companion breed.
VBO:0200345.interestingFact: Hairless and fully coated Powderpuff puppies can be born together, which makes this one of the clearest examples of a single breed containing two striking coat expressions.
VBO:0200345.historicalRoots: Long-established hairless companion type developed under British patronage from dogs associated with China.

VBO:0200389.summary: The Coton de Tulear is a small Madagascar companion whose name says almost everything about its first impression: “coton” for the soft, cotton-like coat, and Tulear for the port city now called Toliara. Beneath all that white texture is a compact dog with a sturdy rather than fragile outline.
VBO:0200389.interestingFact: The breed’s place-name survived a spelling change: Tulear is the older French name for today’s Toliara in southwestern Madagascar.
VBO:0200389.historicalRoots: Companion breed associated with Madagascar and the port of Tulear/Toliara.

VBO:0200406.summary: The Dachshund is a German earthdog built around one unforgettable idea: a long, powerful body carried low enough to follow quarry underground. The name literally points to badger work, while the breed’s three coats and multiple sizes create a surprisingly broad family of looks within that famous silhouette.
VBO:0200406.interestingFact: “Dachshund” translates roughly to “badger dog,” a reminder that the short legs were working equipment before they became an icon.
VBO:0200406.historicalRoots: German hunting dog developed for work below ground.

VBO:0200526.summary: The Finnish Spitz is a fox-red Nordic hunting dog with a bright expression, square outline, and plume of a tail. Its traditional work is unusually audible: rather than silently retrieving game, the dog locates tree-dwelling birds and uses its voice to hold a hunter’s attention on the right spot.
VBO:0200526.interestingFact: In traditional bird hunting, the dog’s rapid barking is part of the method—not a side effect—and skilled barking has even become the subject of competitions in Finland.
VBO:0200526.historicalRoots: Finnish spitz-type hunting dog used to indicate game birds in trees.

VBO:0200610.summary: The Golden Retriever combines a soft, feathered outline with a very practical sporting history. Developed in nineteenth-century Scotland to retrieve game across land and water, it was selected for a useful coat and a gentle carrying mouth. Modern standards often prize an eager, friendly manner, but no breed label predicts every individual dog.
VBO:0200610.interestingFact: The breed’s development is unusually well documented in the records of the Guisachan estate in the Scottish Highlands.
VBO:0200610.historicalRoots: Nineteenth-century Scottish retriever developed for land-and-water gundog work.

VBO:0200623.summary: The Great Dane is a giant with an elegant outline and a habit of making ordinary furniture look miniature. Developed in Germany from large hunting and estate dogs, it became better known as a companion with a statuesque presence. “Gentle giant” is a popular nickname—not a promise about every individual, but an affectionate clue to the breed’s modern image.
VBO:0200623.interestingFact: Despite the English name, the modern breed was developed in Germany, where it is called Deutsche Dogge.
VBO:0200623.historicalRoots: German giant dog descended from large hunting and estate types.

VBO:0200670.summary: The Himalayan Sheepdog is better understood as a regional livestock-guardian population than as one perfectly uniform show-ring breed. Across Himalayan communities, large mountain dogs have worked around flocks, homes, and difficult terrain for generations. Coat, size, and local names can vary, so this portrait is an introduction rather than a single definitive template.
VBO:0200670.interestingFact: “Himalayan Sheepdog” can cover related regional dogs with different local names and appearances—exactly the kind of diversity a global catalog should preserve instead of flattening.

VBO:0200744.summary: The Jindo is a medium Korean spitz from Jindo Island, clean-lined and athletic with a curled or sickle tail and alert triangular ears. Its island history helped preserve a recognizable local type. Breed traditions often emphasize close bonds and keen awareness, though those descriptions should never be treated as a forecast for one dog.
VBO:0200744.interestingFact: Korea protects the Jindo as a Natural Monument, tying the breed’s identity to Jindo Island as well as to its physical standard.
VBO:0200744.historicalRoots: Korean island spitz associated with Jindo County.

VBO:0200800.summary: The Labrador Retriever began with working water dogs from Newfoundland and was refined as a retriever in Great Britain. Its broad head, strong tail, and weather-resistant coat still advertise that aquatic past. Modern standards often describe an outgoing, biddable sporting dog, while real Labradors—like all dogs—remain individuals.
VBO:0200800.interestingFact: The “otter tail” in breed descriptions is not just decorative: its thick, rounded shape is part of the Labrador’s water-working design.
VBO:0200800.historicalRoots: Newfoundland water-dog roots; developed as a retriever in Great Britain.

VBO:0200919.summary: The Mucuchies is a large, mountain-built Venezuelan dog associated with the high Andes around Mérida. Its mostly white coat and sturdy guardian outline suit a breed remembered alongside farms, flocks, and national history. Because populations have been limited, modern preservation is an important part of the story.
VBO:0200919.interestingFact: Nevado, a dog traditionally described as a Mucuchies, became famous as a companion of Simón Bolívar and appears in the breed’s national folklore.
VBO:0200919.historicalRoots: Venezuelan Andean farm and livestock-guardian dog.

VBO:0200934.summary: The New Guinea Singing Dog is a small, agile canine lineage known for flexible movement, a wedge-shaped head, and extraordinary vocalizations. Its relationship to free-ranging New Guinea dogs and long-managed captive populations makes the story more complicated than a conventional modern breed. This is a living biological and cultural history, not just an unusual pet profile.
VBO:0200934.interestingFact: Its famous call rises and shifts in pitch in a way listeners often compare to singing, and groups can blend their voices into striking choruses.
VBO:0200934.historicalRoots: New Guinea free-ranging dog lineage represented by both wild-associated and captive populations.

VBO:0200938.summary: The Newfoundland is a giant Canadian water dog with a massive frame, webbed feet, and a dense coat made for cold, wet work. Its history includes hauling, retrieving, and dramatic water rescues. Breed standards often describe a notably steady expression and manner, though even the most beloved reputation cannot define every individual.
VBO:0200938.interestingFact: A Newfoundland’s swimming style uses a powerful down-and-out stroke that can look more like a breaststroke than the usual dog paddle.
VBO:0200938.historicalRoots: Canadian working water dog associated with Newfoundland fisheries and rescue work.

VBO:0201004.summary: The Peruvian Hairless Dog is an ancient Peruvian companion with a sleek, spare silhouette and skin that makes every line visible. Hairless and coated dogs can both occur, and the breed comes in more than one size. Archaeological images show similarly hairless dogs long before the modern standard gave them a formal frame.
VBO:0201004.interestingFact: Pre-Columbian ceramics from several Peruvian cultures depict hairless dogs, giving the type an unusually visible archaeological trail.
VBO:0201004.historicalRoots: Ancient Peruvian hairless-dog tradition documented in pre-Columbian art.

VBO:0201102.summary: The Puli is a compact Hungarian herding dog whose dense coat can form long cords, turning motion into a spectacular swish of texture. Underneath is a nimble, square-built worker rather than a walking mop. The cords are a coat structure, not a costume, and maintaining them is a serious piece of grooming craft.
VBO:0201102.interestingFact: A mature corded coat forms as the soft undercoat and coarser outer coat intertwine; owners separate the cords by hand rather than brushing them flat.
VBO:0201102.historicalRoots: Hungarian herding dog used around sheep.

VBO:0201135.summary: The Rhodesian Ridgeback is a large southern African hound with one unmistakable signature: a narrow ridge of hair running forward along the back. Developed from European dogs and ridged local dogs, it was used for varied farm and hunting work. Its athletic outline tells that history without turning past function into a claim about modern temperament.
VBO:0201135.interestingFact: The ridge is made by hair growing in the opposite direction from the rest of the coat and is defined by a pair of symmetrical crowns near the shoulders.
VBO:0201135.historicalRoots: Southern African multipurpose hound developed from imported and local ridged dogs.

VBO:0201171.summary: The Saluki is a tall Middle Eastern sighthound whose long history is written in a light frame, deep chest, and effortless-looking stride. Both feathered and smooth coats occur. Across a vast region, related local types were valued for hunting by sight, so the breed’s story is broader than any single country or coat color.
VBO:0201171.interestingFact: The familiar feathered ears are only one expression of the breed: smooth Salukis carry the same elegant structure without the long furnishings.
VBO:0201171.historicalRoots: Ancient Middle Eastern sighthound tradition spanning multiple regions and local types.

VBO:0201220.summary: The Shiba Inu is the smallest of Japan’s native spitz breeds, with a compact frame, curled tail, and an expression that can move from solemn to mischievous in a heartbeat. It was historically used for hunting in mountainous terrain. Standards often prize alertness and independence, but those words are context—not a personality guarantee.
VBO:0201220.interestingFact: The origin of “Shiba” is debated: it may refer to brushwood, an old regional word for small, or the reddish color of autumn brush.
VBO:0201220.historicalRoots: Japanese native hunting spitz associated with mountainous regions.

VBO:0201280.summary: The Spanish Water Dog is a rustic, curly-coated worker from Spain with a long résumé: herding, water work, and help around farms and fishing communities. Its coat can form cords when left to grow, giving the dog a graphic, woolly outline. The versatility is historical; an individual still needs to be met on its own terms.
VBO:0201280.interestingFact: Traditional coat care avoids sculpting the curls into a showy shape—the coat is usually clipped to one even length and allowed to grow naturally.
VBO:0201280.historicalRoots: Spanish multipurpose working dog used for herding and water-related tasks.

VBO:0201348.summary: The Thai Ridgeback is a lean, muscular dog from Thailand with a short coat and a ridge running against the grain along its back. Geographic isolation helped preserve a distinctive local type with upright ears and a clean, athletic silhouette. Modern dogs can vary, but the ridge remains the breed’s visual headline.
VBO:0201348.interestingFact: Only a small group of breeds carries a dorsal hair ridge; in the Thai Ridgeback, its shape can vary from a narrow needle to broader leaf-like patterns.
VBO:0201348.historicalRoots: Long-established Thai ridged dog associated with eastern regions of the country.

VBO:0201421.summary: The Whippet is a medium British sighthound: all sweeping curves, tucked waist, and surprising acceleration. It became closely associated with working-class racing and rabbit coursing, earning the affectionate nickname “the poor man’s racehorse.” At rest the outline can look delicate; in motion it makes perfect mechanical sense.
VBO:0201421.interestingFact: Whippets were once raced down straight tracks toward a waving cloth, a working-class sport that helped shape both the breed and its enduring speed-dog image.
VBO:0201421.historicalRoots: British sighthound developed for racing and small-game coursing.

VBO:0201436.summary: The Xoloitzcuintli—usually shortened to Xolo—is an ancient Mexican breed with both hairless and coated varieties and three recognized sizes. The hairless form reveals every elegant angle, while the coated form is a reminder that the breed is more genetically and visually varied than its best-known image suggests.
VBO:0201436.interestingFact: Its name joins Xolotl, an Aztec deity, with itzcuintli, a Nahuatl word for dog; saying “Xolo” is the friendly shortcut.
VBO:0201436.historicalRoots: Ancient Mexican dog represented in pre-Columbian culture and modern hairless and coated forms.
